Coefficient Alpha With a Confidence Interval

Source: R/reliability_alpha.R
reliability_alpha.Rd

Estimates coefficient \(\alpha\) for a homogeneous composite score and returns a confidence interval for the population coefficient using one of several documented methods.

Usage

reliability_alpha(
  data = NULL,
  S = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  estimator = c("analytic", "model_implied"),
  missing = c("fiml", "listwise", "two_stage"),
  aux = NULL,
  ci_method = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  B = 10000,
  seed = NULL,
  ncpus = 1L,
  improper = c("keep", "drop"),
  wald_df = Inf,
  progress = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A numeric matrix or data frame of item scores (rows are respondents, columns are items). Either data or S must be supplied. How incomplete rows are handled is governed by missing: full information maximum likelihood by default, listwise deletion with missing = "listwise", or two-stage maximum likelihood with missing = "two_stage". When aux is supplied, data contains both the item columns and the auxiliary columns, and the columns not named in aux are the items. An item column that is not numeric (or logical), and an item that takes a single value in the rows analyzed (the complete rows under listwise deletion, the rows that observe it otherwise), are refused by name before anything is computed, as is a zero variance on the diagonal of S: such an item adds a constant to the composite, whose reliability it leaves as it is, while the coefficient would count it among the \(J\) items (alpha with it is \(J(J-2)/(J-1)^2\) times alpha without it). A composite that does not vary is refused too, as when the items are ipsative (their scores sum to the same total in every row): its reliability is not defined. Under missing = "fiml" and "two_stage" it is checked in the rows that observe every item when they outnumber the items, where a composite that does not vary leaves the likelihood of the saturated model without a maximum, and otherwise on the EM estimate of the covariance matrix. SPSS user-defined missing values, which haven::read_sav(user_na = TRUE) keeps as values of a haven_labelled_spss column, are missing, as SPSS treats them.

S

A symmetric covariance matrix among the items. If S is supplied, N must also be supplied; raw-data-only confidence interval methods ("adf", "bootstrap_*", "percentile", "bca") are then unavailable, as are missing = "fiml" and missing = "two_stage" named explicitly, and aux, since a covariance matrix has no incomplete cases (the default of missing analyzes it as it stands).

N

Total sample size; required when S (rather than data) is supplied.

estimator

How \(\alpha\) is estimated: "analytic" (the default) applies the closed-form equation to the observed covariance matrix, and "model_implied" takes the reliability implied by the \(\tau\)-equivalent single-factor model fit by maximum likelihood. See Details.

missing

How incomplete rows of data are handled: "fiml" (the default; full information maximum likelihood, using every case with at least one observed item or observed auxiliary variable), "listwise" (complete-case analysis), or "two_stage" (two-stage maximum likelihood, using the same cases as FIML). The default analysis is FIML whenever an item value is missing and the complete data analysis otherwise, unlike fa_confirmatory, which fits complete data by FIML too: data in which no value is missing, data complete but for rows with every item missing (which both treatments drop), and S are analyzed as they stand, with the complete data default interval, since the complete-data intervals need that analysis; incomplete items are analyzed by FIML, or, when ci_method names an interval FIML cannot give, the call stops and names the choices. See Details. With missing = "listwise", when fewer than two rows are complete, listwise deletion leaves nothing to analyze, and the function stops before any fit, says so, and names the treatment that uses the incomplete rows. The analytic estimator needs only the trace and the sum of the covariance matrix, which any two rows give, so it is computed from two or more complete rows. The model implied estimator fits the single-factor model by maximum likelihood, which needs the covariance matrix positive definite, and \(N\) complete rows give a matrix of rank at most \(N - 1\); with no more complete rows than items it stops before the fit, says why, and names the treatment that uses the incomplete rows. Ordinary FIML is evaluated by the observed values and missingness patterns, not a blanket count of complete cases. Analytic alpha and two-stage estimation need unrestricted moments. The likelihood diagnostic refuses a certified affine-collapse direction or a numerical affine instability, as described in cov_fiml; EM convergence alone does not establish existence or uniqueness. Model-implied alpha can retain a proper identified constrained FIML fit with H0-based errors when H1 diagnostics are unavailable; the returned result states this limit. The complete rows behind the model-implied listwise estimator are counted as distinct rows. Bootstrap resamples retain a separate distinct-case estimability screen, which is a policy, not a proof that every smaller constrained FIML likelihood is unbounded. The refusal message for the analytic estimator names listwise deletion when two or more rows are complete and listwise deletion would accept them, and otherwise says why it cannot help either. A refusal of listwise deletion names missing = "fiml" only when that method could use the data, so the two refusals never point at each other, and when two columns share a name (which listwise deletion without aux reads by position, and that method refuses) it says to name them apart first.

aux

Optional character vector naming auxiliary variable columns of data: entered as saturated correlates under full information maximum likelihood, and into the first stage under missing = "two_stage". Supplying aux without missing implies missing = "fiml". See Details.

ci_method

Method for constructing the confidence interval. See Details for which methods each estimator supports. The default NULL resolves to "bonett" for the analytic estimator and to "mlr" for the model implied estimator (or "ml" when only a covariance matrix is supplied, since "mlr" needs raw data). Under FIML (the default of missing with incomplete items) and two-stage estimation the analytic default is "ml", whose standard error comes from the information matrix of the saturated model; with complete data the default of missing keeps "bonett".

conf_level

Confidence level for the interval (1 - Type I error rate). Defaults to 0.95.

B

Number of bootstrap replications when a bootstrap method is selected, a single whole number. Defaults to 10000. The fewest accepted depends on the interval method and the level: at the default conf_level, 400 for "percentile" (10 replications beyond each limit), 2000 for "bca" (50 beyond each nominal limit, because the adjusted limits sit farther into the tails), and 100 for "bootstrap_se" and "bootstrap_se_logistic" (a standard deviation of the replications); at 0.99 the first two are 2000 and 10000. A smaller B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). The count is held to the number requested. Replications set aside afterward are counted and reported in a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped, which names the function and says to request more when those that return a value are fewer than the number required; when fewer than half of the B replications return a value, the interval is withheld (limits and bootstrap standard error NA) under a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. See dmar_bootstrap, which also describes options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) for a first look with a smaller B.

seed

Random number seed used for bootstrap reproducibility. Defaults to NULL, under which the resamples are drawn from, and advance, the current random number stream; supply an integer for a reproducible interval. When set, the seed applies inside the function only, and the user's generator state is restored when the function returns.

ncpus

The number of processes over which the bootstrap replications are spread. The default 1 runs them in this R session; a larger number uses forked workers (boot's parallel = "multicore") or, on Windows, which cannot fork, a socket cluster ("snow"), whose workers load the installed DMAR. boot draws every resample before any replication runs, so a given seed returns the same interval, counts, and replicates whatever ncpus is. A session that forks workers and also starts background processes through callr or processx needs the environment variable PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD set before processx is loaded (see sem_exact_fit_bootstrap). Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

improper

For estimator = "model_implied" with a bootstrap interval: how a replication whose tau-equivalent single-factor solution is improper (a negative error variance, a Heywood case) is treated when the solution still yields a coefficient. "keep" (the default) uses its estimate like any other, and "drop" sets it aside; either way such replications are counted, and one whose solution yields no coefficient is set aside under both. With "drop" an improper point estimate stops the call. See reliability_omega for the reasoning. The analytic estimator fits no model, so no replication of it can be improper, and the argument has no effect there beyond being recorded as the improper_rule of the bootstrap attribute.

wald_df

The degrees of freedom of the t distribution to which a Wald interval refers: Inf (the default) is the normal reference, and a single positive number replaces the normal quantile with the t quantile on that many degrees of freedom. It applies to "ml", "mlr", "adf", and their _logistic variants; a finite value with any other interval is an error. The keyword "missing_information" of reliability_omega is an error here: its calibration found that the t reference gives alpha's FIML interval no gain and too much coverage. See Details.

progress

NULL (the default), or a function of two arguments that the bootstrap calls as it runs, so that an application can show how far a long bootstrap has gone and let its user stop it (a Shiny app, for example). It is called as progress(done, total), with the number of replications attempted so far and B: after each replication when ncpus = 1, and with more processes after each block of replications they complete together, about a fiftieth of B (ncpus * ceiling(B / (50 * ncpus)) replications, the last block possibly fewer), so that done advances by the block. A BCa interval takes its acceleration from a regression on the resampling frequencies when at least as many replications return a value as there are cases, and from the jackknife, one leave-one-out refit per case, when fewer do or when that regression fails or gives influence values that are not all finite; the jackknife runs at most once in a call, and not at all when no interval is formed or every returned replicate has the same value. While it runs, the callback is called again after each refit (with more processes, after each block of ncpus * ceiling(n / (50 * ncpus)) refits, n the number of cases resampled), with done and total both B, so it can be called more than B times, and done equal to total does not mean that the bootstrap has finished. If the callback returns FALSE, the bootstrap stops before the next replication or block with an error of class dmar_bootstrap_cancelled, whose elements done and total say how far it got (see dmar_metadata); any other value is ignored. An error inside the callback stops the call with an error of class dmar_progress_error, whose message names the callback and which carries done, total, and, as parent, the callback's own condition with its class intact, so that an application can tell a failing callback from a failing analysis. The callback runs outside the random number stream, so a given seed returns the same result with or without it, and a callback that draws random numbers leaves the caller's stream as it found it. With NULL nothing is called. Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value and rows "estimate" (sample coefficient \(\alpha\)), "se" (standard error on the coefficient scale, NA for methods that do not produce one; for the transformation-based intervals "fisher", "bonett", and "hakstian_whalen" it is the delta method back-transform of the transformation-scale standard error, evaluated at the estimate), "se_transformed" (only for those transformation-based intervals: the standard error on the transformation scale, the quantity the interval is built from, with the scale named in the attribute se_transform_scale: "fisher_z", "log(1-alpha)", or "cube_root"), "ci_lower" and "ci_upper" (each clamped into [0, 1], so the limits stay in order), "conf_level", "N" (the cases the analysis used: the complete cases under listwise deletion, and under "fiml" and "two_stage" every case with at least one observed item or observed auxiliary variable), "N_complete" (the complete cases, so the cost of listwise deletion is visible at a glance; equal to "N" under listwise deletion and for covariance input), and "n_items" (number of items). The selected coefficient, CI method, and missing-data treatment travel as the attributes coefficient, ci_method, missing, wald_df (the degrees of freedom of the Wald interval's t reference, Inf for the normal one and for intervals that are not Wald intervals), and (when supplied) aux; bootstrap calls also record B. A bootstrap call also carries the attribute bootstrap, a list recording the replications the interval conditions on: attempted (B), returned (the replications whose value the interval uses; the standard error is their standard deviation and the percentile and BCa limits are their quantiles), failed (the difference), reasons (a named count of why replications were set aside: error when the refit raised an error, non_finite when it was set aside without one, as a fit that did not converge is, and as an improper one is under improper = "drop" even though its estimate is finite), error_messages (the distinct error messages with their counts, empty when none), undetermined (the replications set aside because the resample left a polychoric correlation undetermined, which only reliability_omega_categorical counts; zero here), improper and improper_kept (the replications whose tau-equivalent single-factor solution, under estimator = "model_implied", was improper, with a negative error variance: those set aside, which are among the non_finite ones, and those whose estimate the interval uses, which are among the returned ones), no_solution (zero here: it counts the replications of three items with no congeneric single-factor solution, which reliability_omega meets), improper_rule ("keep" or "drop"; see the argument improper), not_converged (zero here: a fit that did not converge is counted among the non_finite ones), too_few_cases (the replications set aside because the resample held too few distinct cases for the rule on the number of cases, which are among the error ones; when they number more than half of B, no interval is formed), caution (TRUE when the replications set aside and the improper ones kept number at least \((1 - C)/2\) of B, with \(C\) the confidence level, so that how they were treated can decide where a limit falls), require_half (TRUE: an interval requires at least half of all attempted replications to return defined estimates; this is an estimability safeguard, not a coverage guarantee), required (the fewest replications a request for an interval of this method and level may ask for, a count held to B and not to the replications that return a value: 400 for "percentile", 2000 for "bca", 100 for the two bootstrap standard error methods at the 95 percent level; see dmar_bootstrap), bootstrap_status ("complete", "dropped", "exploratory", "insufficient_count", or "insufficient_share"; under the last two the limits are NA), B_used (the smallest count any reported limit rests on), target_returned and target_withheld (counts and withholding flags for each target in a vector bootstrap), acceleration and acceleration_method (the BCa acceleration used and whether it came from the regression or the jackknife; NA unless a BCa interval was formed), jackknife (the same attempted, returned, failed, reasons, error_messages, undetermined, improper, improper_kept, no_solution, not_converged, and too_few_cases for the leave-one-out refits behind the acceleration, all zero when no jackknife ran), ncpus (the number of processes used), t (the estimate of every replication, in order, NA where there is none; an improper estimate set aside under improper = "drop" is kept here, so the interval under the other rule can be formed without refitting), and status (a factor giving the fate of every replication, with levels "proper", "improper", "error", "non_finite", "undetermined", and "not_converged"). The interval uses the replications whose status is "proper" and, under improper = "keep", those whose status is "improper" and whose t is finite. The attribute B_used is the number of replications the interval uses (returned). The attributes n_dropped (B minus B_used), B_required, and bootstrap_status repeat the counts in the names every bootstrap result of the package carries. The warning has class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped when replications were set aside and the interval was formed, and dmar_bootstrap_insufficient when the interval was withheld. A BCa interval is also withheld, with the second class, when fewer than 10 replications lie beyond a limit where the bias correction and the acceleration place it (see dmar_bootstrap). The printed table shows these counts in one line, and a warning states them whenever a replication was set aside or the caution applies.

Details

Coefficient \(\alpha\) was first derived by Guttman (1945) as his \(\lambda_3\) and was subsequently popularized by Cronbach (1951), under whose name the coefficient is often informally cited. The attribution to Cronbach is historically incomplete; the modern literature increasingly refers to the coefficient simply as “coefficient alpha” (see, e.g., Sijtsma, 2009; Revelle & Zinbarg, 2009). DMAR follows that convention.

For a \(J\)-item composite \(Y = \sum_j X_j\) the population coefficient is $$\alpha = \frac{J}{J-1}\left(1 - \frac{\sum_{j} \sigma_{j}^{2}}{\sigma_{Y}^{2}}\right),$$ where \(\sigma_{j}^{2}\) is the variance of item j and \(\sigma_{Y}^{2}\) is the variance of the composite. The sample estimate substitutes sample variances. Under classical test theory, \(\alpha\) equals the population reliability of the composite when the items are essentially \(\tau\)-equivalent (i.e., equal factor loadings); when loadings differ, \(\alpha\) is a lower bound on the population reliability. For well-behaved homogeneous measurement instruments coefficient \(\alpha\) and McDonald's (1999) coefficient \(\omega\) (reliability_omega) typically yield very similar values; \(\omega\) extends to congeneric items (heterogeneous loadings) without the lower-bound caveat. For ordered categorical items see reliability_omega_categorical.

Coefficient \(\alpha\) is at most one but, as a function of the covariance matrix, has no lower bound: it falls below zero when the item covariances are negative on balance, which can arise when an item is scored in the opposite direction to the others and needs reverse scoring. A reliability coefficient cannot be negative, so a negative estimate is returned as computed, with a warning that says so, and each confidence limit is clamped into [0, 1]; the interval around an estimate far enough below zero is then [0, 0], which says that the data support no positive reliability for the items as keyed.

Two estimators of the same coefficient. The argument estimator selects how \(\alpha\) is estimated from the data. Both target the same population quantity, and they agree in the population whenever the \(\tau\)-equivalent model holds; they differ in a finite sample because they take different routes to it.

"analytic"

The default. The closed-form equation above, applied to the observed covariance matrix. This is the classical coefficient, the number a hand calculation produces, and it makes no assumption beyond those of classical test theory.

"model_implied"

The reliability implied by the \(\tau\)-equivalent (equal loadings) single-factor model fit by maximum likelihood. With a shared loading \(\lambda\) and error variances \(\psi_j^{2}\) the model implied reliability of the \(J\)-item composite is $$\alpha = \frac{(J \lambda)^{2}}{(J \lambda)^{2} + \sum_{j} \psi_{j}^{2}},$$ with maximum likelihood estimates substituted. Estimating through the model brings inference the formula cannot provide: a delta method standard error, a robust (Satorra-Bentler) variant under nonnormality, the profile likelihood interval, and a fit assessment of the \(\tau\)-equivalence claim itself. When the equal-loadings claim is doubtful, the congeneric reliability_omega is the appropriate coefficient rather than either \(\alpha\).

Users of MBESS will recognize these as ci.reliability(type = "alpha") and ci.reliability(type = "alpha-cfa") respectively.

Missing data and auxiliary variables. Listwise deletion is unbiased only when the data are missing completely at random and is inefficient always; the mlmr vignette develops the argument at length. By default (missing = "fiml") incomplete data are therefore analyzed by full information maximum likelihood (FIML), which keeps every case with at least one observed item and is consistent and efficient under the weaker missing at random (MAR) assumption; missing = "listwise" analyzes the complete rows alone. Data in which no value is missing, and a covariance matrix, are analyzed as they stand: FIML would give the same coefficient, and the interval is the complete data one, Bonett's by default for the analytic estimator. A row with every item missing does not count as incomplete data: without auxiliary variables, listwise deletion and FIML both drop it, so data that are complete but for such rows (a blank line at the end of a spreadsheet, say) are analyzed as they stand too. The default analysis is therefore FIML whenever an item value is missing and the complete data analysis otherwise. fa_confirmatory differs: it fits complete data by FIML as well. The complete data analysis is used here because the closed-form intervals ("bonett", "feldt", "fisher", "hakstian_whalen"), "adf", "adf_logistic", and "likelihood" need it, FIML giving none of them. When the default meets incomplete items and one of those intervals, the call stops rather than deleting cases unasked, and names the two choices: missing = "listwise", which computes the interval from the complete rows alone, or an interval FIML gives for the estimator in use ("ml", "ml_logistic", with the model implied estimator "mlr" and "mlr_logistic", or a bootstrap method); when ci_method is not supplied, the analytic estimator's interval under FIML is "ml". The aux argument names auxiliary variables: columns of data that are not part of the composite but are correlated with the items or with the reasons values are missing. They are entered as saturated correlates (Graham, 2003): correlated freely with each other and with every item's residual, never loading on the factor and never entering the composite, so the measurement model is undisturbed while FIML uses their information. Beyond recovering information, a good auxiliary makes the MAR assumption itself more plausible, since missingness that depends on the auxiliary becomes MAR once the auxiliary is conditioned on (Collins, Schafer, & Kam, 2001). A case whose items are all missing is kept when an auxiliary variable is observed on it: the saturated model estimates the items and the auxiliaries jointly, so such a case informs the item moments through its auxiliaries, and setting it aside would make the analysis conditional on having an observed item, which biases the estimates when the items go missing together at random given the auxiliaries. Supplying aux without missing implies missing = "fiml", whether or not a value is missing; combining it with an explicit missing = "listwise" is an error. How each estimator uses FIML: the model implied estimator simply fits its model with missing = "ml"; the analytic estimator applies the classical formula, unchanged, to the FIML estimate of the item covariance matrix (the EM estimate under a saturated model over the items and any auxiliaries, the matrix cov_fiml returns), so the estimand stays the classical coefficient and only the covariance matrix it is computed from improves. Under missing = "fiml" the available intervals are "ml" and "ml_logistic" (both estimators; the standard error comes from the FIML information matrix), "mlr" and "mlr_logistic" (model implied estimator; the Yuan-Bentler robust standard error), and the bootstrap methods, which resample rows (including the partially observed ones) and refit by FIML on each replication. The complete-data closed forms ("feldt", "fisher", "bonett", "hakstian_whalen"), "adf", and "likelihood" are errors with missing = "fiml" rather than silently reverting to listwise deletion.

missing = "two_stage" estimates in two stages (Yuan & Bentler, 2000; Savalei & Bentler, 2009): the means and covariances of the items are first estimated by maximum likelihood under the saturated normal model (the EM estimates, with any aux variables entering this stage only), and the model is then fit to them by the complete data maximum likelihood discrepancy function. The analytic coefficient is a function of the first stage alone, which is the saturated maximum likelihood estimate FIML uses too, so its value and its intervals are those of missing = "fiml" computed from the same cases. Those are the cases FIML uses: every case with an observed item or, with aux, an observed auxiliary variable, since the first stage estimates the items and the auxiliaries jointly and a case observed on an auxiliary alone informs the item moments through it. Setting such a case aside would condition the analysis on an observed item and bias the estimates when the items went missing together at random given the auxiliaries. lavaan's two-stage estimator reads such a case in its first stage but leaves it out of its sample size, which would make its standard errors too large; the model implied fits go through fa_confirmatory, which computes them again with every case the first stage read, and a message counts such cases (when a fit cannot be computed again, a warning says that the standard error is too large and that a bootstrap interval counts every case). The model implied coefficient comes from the tau-equivalent model fit in the second stage, with the normal theory two-stage standard error (Savalei & Bentler, 2009, Eq. 6) for "ml" and the one robust to nonnormality (Yuan & Bentler, 2000; Savalei & Falk, 2014) for "mlr". The intervals FIML refuses are refused here too, "likelihood" also because no likelihood of the observed data is maximized. Multiple imputation is a different feature with a different interface and is out of scope here.

Both methods need the covariance of every pair of items and auxiliary variables, and the data carry no information about the covariance of a pair that no case observes together: lavaan only warns, and its EM returns an arbitrary value for it. Nor do they carry any about how two variables vary together when the cases that observe both hold a single value of one of them (or are one case): the estimate of their covariance then rests on the form of the normal model rather than on the data, or is not determined at all. Either pair is refused by name before any fit, with a pointer to missing_coverage, and a refusal of listwise deletion offers missing = "fiml" only when the data hold no such pair. In a bootstrap, a resample that leaves such a pair (or, for the BCa acceleration, a jackknife deletion that does) is set aside with the same message and counted, under either method.

Available confidence interval methods (set via ci_method). Some belong to one estimator only, because a closed-form interval for the sample coefficient and a model-based interval are not interchangeable; requesting a method the chosen estimator cannot supply is an error that names the estimator to use instead:

"feldt"

Analytic estimator only. The F-distribution interval of Feldt (1965), exact under multivariate normality and parallel items.

"fisher"

Analytic estimator only. Fisher's \(z'\) transformation (Fisher, 1950). Tends to overcover (Padilla, Divers, & Newton, 2012) and is generally not recommended.

"bonett"

Analytic estimator only. Bonett's (2002) log transformation. The default for that estimator; well-behaved under normality.

"hakstian_whalen"

Analytic estimator only. Cube-root transformation of Hakstian and Whalen (1976).

"mlr", "mlr_logistic"

Model implied estimator only. Wald interval using the robust (Satorra & Bentler, 1994) standard error from the fitted model. The default for that estimator; recommended among the closed forms when item distributions deviate from normality (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016). Requires raw data.

"likelihood"

Model implied estimator only. Profile likelihood interval: the set of population values not rejected by the likelihood ratio test under the \(\tau\)-equivalent model, located by refitting under the nonlinear constraint that the model implied reliability equals each candidate value. Respects [0, 1], is not forced to be symmetric, and works from raw data or covariance input. Requires lavaan. It is unavailable with the analytic estimator because the interval and the point estimate would then refer to different quantities: the interval profiles the model implied coefficient while the estimate is the sample coefficient, so under a misspecified model the interval can exclude the estimate it accompanies.

"ml", "ml_logistic"

Available to both estimators, by the route each affords. With "analytic" it is the closed-form ML standard error of van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel (2000), computed directly from the covariance matrix; with "model_implied" it is the delta method standard error from the fitted model. The _logistic variant applies Browne's (1982) logit transformation.

"adf", "adf_logistic"

Available to both estimators. With "analytic" it is the asymptotic distribution-free standard error of Maydeu-Olivares, Coffman, and Hartmann (2007); with "model_implied" the model is fit by weighted least squares (Browne, 1984) and the delta method applied. Requires raw data and a relatively large sample size.

"bootstrap_se", "bootstrap_se_logistic", "percentile", "bca"

Available to both estimators. Nonparametric bootstrap intervals (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993): the rows of data are resampled with replacement B times and the chosen estimator is recomputed on each replication. "percentile" takes the interval limits from the empirical quantiles of the bootstrap estimates (for a 95 percent interval, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles); it respects [0, 1] and is not forced to be symmetric about the estimate, but its coverage degrades when the estimator is biased or its variance changes with the parameter. "bca" (bias-corrected and accelerated) adjusts the two quantile positions for exactly those features, estimating the median bias from the bootstrap distribution and the acceleration from the jackknife, and is second-order accurate where the percentile interval is first-order accurate (DiCiccio & Efron, 1996). The acceleration is estimated as boot estimates it, by regression on the resampling frequencies when at least as many replications as cases returned a value and by the jackknife otherwise, or when that regression fails; a leave-one-out refit that fails is counted and set aside rather than stopping the call, and when the acceleration or the bias correction cannot be estimated at all the percentile interval is returned in its place, with a warning and the substitution recorded in the ci_method attribute; see reliability_omega_categorical for the full account. "bootstrap_se" uses the standard deviation of the bootstrap estimates as a standard error in an ordinary normal-theory interval; the _logistic variant builds that interval on the logit scale so the endpoints respect [0, 1], with the standard deviation carried to that scale by the delta method, divided by \(\hat\alpha(1 - \hat\alpha)\), as in Equation 32 of Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) and in MBESS::ci.reliability(). When every replication returns the same value, as when every item is an exact linear function of the same variable (an item entered twice beside other items does not do it), the bootstrap distribution is a single point and every method returns that point at both limits, with a warning; so does the _logistic variant at a value of one (identical items), where the logit is infinite. Replications on which the estimator cannot be computed (for example, a model refit that does not converge) are set aside, and so is a replication in which an item takes a single value (a resample that has left out every case on which a rare item differs from the rest, or the jackknife deletion of such a case), which is refused as the data would be, by name. A replication follows the rule on the number of cases as the data do (see missing): a resample repeats rows, and one with no more distinct cases than the rule asks for is set aside, so near the rule's bound many are (at 12 cases and eight variables, about three resamples in four). When more than half are, no interval is reported (the standard error and the limits are NA): the replications left hold more distinct cases than a resample typically does, so their spread understates the sampling variability of the coefficient, and at the bound itself each holds every distinct case and, without repeated rows, gives the estimate. Without repeated rows that happens at fewer cases than about 1.65 times the count the rule compares them with (fewer than 14 for eight variables). The interval is computed from the replications that return a value, whose quantiles the percentile and BCa limits are; the counts, and why the rest were set aside, travel in the bootstrap attribute (see Value), print under the table, and are stated in a warning whenever a replication was set aside. Requires raw data and the boot package. The default B = 10000 is an accuracy choice: the BCa adjustment pushes the working quantiles farther into the tails of the bootstrap distribution than the percentile interval uses, and stabilizing them takes more replications than the customary 2000; reduce B for exploration, not for a reported analysis. Bootstrap results vary from run to run; supply seed for reproducibility, and ncpus to spread the replications over several processes, which leaves the interval for a given seed unchanged. Under estimator = "model_implied" each replication refits the tau-equivalent model by maximum likelihood, whose estimate robust maximum likelihood shares, and a replication whose solution is improper is kept or set aside according to improper, as reliability_omega describes; an improper point estimate whose error variances sum below zero, so that the model implies a negative error variance for the composite, stops with a message rather than returning a coefficient above one. (The likelihood of the tau-equivalent model has a maximum: one item's error variance cannot run off below zero while its loading grows, since the loadings are equal and every covariance would grow with them, so the stop of class dmar_no_maximum that reliability_omega describes does not arise here.)

"none"

Return only the point estimate.

Two complete rows. Coefficient \(\alpha\) needs only the trace and the sum of the covariance matrix, so it is computed from any two rows, but the covariance matrix of two rows has rank one: every pair of items correlates +1 or -1, whatever the items, and the estimate is a function of the difference between the two rows alone. Feldt's interval is exact for any N of at least 2 under multivariate normality and parallel items (for 0/1 items, as in reliability_kr20, it is an approximation; Feldt, 1965), and it is the interval the refusals below name. The Hakstian-Whalen interval is defined there too, but at N = 2 its upper limit lies above one for every data set whose alpha is below one at any confidence level above about .90, and is clamped to one (at an alpha of one, which two rows can give, the interval is \([1, 1]\)). The rest are refused at N = 2, each for its own reason, as "fisher" is below N = 4: Bonett's variance, \(2J/((J-1)(N-2))\), is infinite; the "ml" and "adf" standard errors (and their _logistic variants), which treat that matrix as the population's, are zero for any data (the asymptotic variance of van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel, 2000, vanishes at a matrix of rank one, and each case's centered cross products are then proportional to the covariance matrix, which alpha does not change with); and every bootstrap resample is one row twice or both rows, so the bootstrap distribution has no spread. The model implied estimator needs more complete rows than items (see missing).

A t reference distribution for the Wald intervals. The intervals "ml", "mlr", and "adf", with their _logistic variants, are Wald intervals: the estimate plus or minus a normal quantile times its standard error. The argument wald_df replaces the normal quantile with the t quantile on wald_df degrees of freedom and leaves the estimate and the standard error as they are (von Hippel, 2016, Eq. 29); for the _logistic variants the t quantile is applied on the logit scale. The default, Inf, is the normal reference, and a finite value with any other interval is an error. A number is the analyst's own choice of degrees of freedom, a sensitivity check; reliability_omega discusses it further.

The keyword wald_df = "missing_information", which reliability_omega and fa_confirmatory accept, is an error here. The calibration study behind it (in the package's source repository, methodology/missing_data; fa_confirmatory describes its design) evaluated alpha's FIML interval (missing = "fiml", ci_method = "ml") with normal data, one factor models of six items (N from 30 to 200) or 12 (N = 50 and 100), and 15 or 30 percent of the values of half the items missing. On the normal reference that interval was already close to .95: over the cells with \(N \le 100\) and missing values its coverage was .0043 from .95 on average (between .940 and .958 in every cell). The t reference on von Hippel's \(\max\{3, N(1 - \gamma) - 1\}\) degrees of freedom came barely closer (.0042), and in one cell its coverage reached .966, above the .96 that the study's decision rule, fixed before the run, allowed, so no rule passed. That cell, with 12 items, N = 50, and 30 percent missing completely at random, is the one where the study's fit of the saturated model converged in only 53 percent of the replications (in 100 replications of that design this function's fit, which starts at the EM estimates, converged in 91 and the study's in 49), so the coverage there conditions on the samples the study's fit could handle; without it the t reference would have passed (.0035 against .0042, at most .9595). The verdict is the rule's as fixed in advance, and alpha keeps the normal reference unless a number is given; the t reference would change its interval little in any case. On the logit scale none of von Hippel's four rules passed either. The printed table names the reference distribution in a line under it, and the wald_df attribute records it.

Comparison with other packages. The psych package provides alpha, which reports coefficient \(\alpha\) along with item-level diagnostics (item-total correlations, alpha-if-item-deleted, and several alternative coefficients). The emphasis in psych is broad exploratory psychometric reporting. reliability_alpha in DMAR differs in emphasis: it returns a single point estimate alongside a confidence interval drawn from the methods compared in Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016).

Examples

set.seed(113)
# Simulate six tau-equivalent items with population reliability ~ .8.
J <- 6
loadings <- rep(0.6, J)
eta <- rnorm(200)
errors <- matrix(rnorm(200 * J, sd = sqrt(1 - 0.6^2)), 200, J)
items <- outer(eta, loadings) + errors
colnames(items) <- paste0("y", seq_len(J))

# Default (Bonett's transformation) CI from raw data.
reliability_alpha(data = items)
#>  term           value
#>  estimate       0.777
#>  se             0.025
#>  se_transformed 0.110
#>  ci_lower       0.723
#>  ci_upper       0.820
#>  conf_level     0.950
#>  N              200  
#>  N_complete     200  
#>  n_items        6    

# Same point estimate from a covariance matrix; CI requires N.
S <- cov(items)
reliability_alpha(S = S, N = 200, ci_method = "feldt")
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.777
#>  se         <NA> 
#>  ci_lower   0.725
#>  ci_upper   0.821
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 200  
#>  n_items    6    

# The bootstrap intervals resample the rows and recompute the
# coefficient on each replication. The percentile interval reads its
# limits off the empirical quantiles of the bootstrap estimates.
# B = 500 keeps the example quick (a 95 percent percentile interval
# is reported from 400 or more); a reported interval deserves the
# default B = 10000, and seed makes the interval reproducible.
reliability_alpha(data = items, ci_method = "percentile", B = 500,
                  seed = 113)
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.777
#>  se         0.023
#>  ci_lower   0.730
#>  ci_upper   0.815
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 200  
#>  n_items    6    
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 500 replications attempted, 500 returned a value

# The bias-corrected and accelerated interval adjusts those two
# quantile positions for median bias and for acceleration, and is the
# better choice for a reported interval. The default B = 10000 is an
# accuracy choice, not a formality, since BCa works farther into the
# tails of the bootstrap distribution than the percentile interval
# does (see Details). For the same reason B = 2000 is the fewest
# replications a 95 percent BCa interval is run with.
reliability_alpha(data = items, ci_method = "bca", B = 2000, seed = 113)
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.777
#>  se         0.024
#>  ci_lower   0.725
#>  ci_upper   0.819
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 200  
#>  n_items    6    
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 2000 replications attempted, 2000 returned a value

# An application that runs a long bootstrap (a Shiny app, for example)
# can follow it through a progress callback, which is called with the
# replications attempted so far and B, and can stop it by returning
# FALSE. The callback changes no result: this is the percentile
# interval above.
reliability_alpha(data = items, ci_method = "percentile", B = 500,
                  seed = 113, progress = function(done, total) {
                    if (done %% 250 == 0) message(done, " of ", total)
                  })
#> 250 of 500
#> 500 of 500
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.777
#>  se         0.023
#>  ci_lower   0.730
#>  ci_upper   0.815
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 200  
#>  n_items    6    
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 500 replications attempted, 500 returned a value

# Full information maximum likelihood with an auxiliary variable.
# Missingness on y2 depends on an auxiliary z (missing at random given
# z), so listwise deletion is biased and FIML with z is not. Supplying
# aux implies missing = "fiml"; the N_complete row shows how many
# rows listwise deletion would have kept.
z <- eta + rnorm(200, sd = 0.5)
d <- data.frame(items, z = z)
d$y2[runif(200) < plogis(-1 + 1.5 * as.numeric(scale(z)))] <- NA
reliability_alpha(data = d, aux = "z")
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.776
#>  se         0.025
#>  ci_lower   0.727
#>  ci_upper   0.826
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 140  
#>  n_items    6
